Application Areas: Antimicrobial resistance mechanisms in Gram-positive pathogens
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Polyphasic Taxonomic Delineation: Integrating whole-genome sequencing metrics (ANI, AAI, dDDH) with phenotypic characterization to resolve species boundaries and validate novel prokaryotic lineages, as demonstrated by the description of new *Methylomonas* species and the reclassification of *Terribacillus*.

Cell Wall Homeostasis Mechanism Elucidation: Investigating the regulatory interplay between lipoteichoic acid (LTA) and peptidoglycan hydrolases (e.g., ScaH) to understand cell wall integrity, osmoresistance, and beta-lactam resistance in *Staphylococcus aureus*.

Rigorous Anaerobic Cultivation Strategy: Employing modified Balch and Hungate techniques with precise redox potential control and anoxic gas phase management to isolate and maintain strict anaerobes from diverse environments, ensuring physiological relevance for downstream genomic and metabolic analysis.

Sequence-Based Nomenclature Frameworks: Advocating for and implementing the SeqCode alongside traditional ICNP standards to enable valid naming of uncultured microbes via metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) while maintaining culture-based validation for phenotypic accuracy.
Summary Description: Paul A. Lawson is a microbial taxonomist and molecular microbiologist specializing in the systematic classification of prokaryotes and the physiological mechanisms of Gram-positive pathogens. His research integrates whole-genome sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and rigorous phenotypic characterization to delineate new species, particularly methanotrophs and environmental bacteria. Concurrently, he investigates cell wall biology in *Staphylococcus aureus*, focusing on lipoteichoic acid-mediated regulation of peptidoglycan hydrolases to combat antimicrobial resistance. Lawson also contributes significantly to microbial nomenclature frameworks, bridging culture-dependent and sequence-based taxonomic standards, while advancing anaerobic cultivation techniques for environmental and clinical isolates.
